title: The boy bent in eight places
hookLine: a boy bent in eight places walks into a king's court, and the court laughs
carry: the self is not the skin

lines: A BOY GOES TO THE KING'S COURT.
cards: An unborn child corrects his own father. The Mahabharata tells of a scholar named Kahoda who recited the Vedas while his wife was pregnant, and from inside the womb the child pointed out his mistakes.

The father, stung, cursed him: you'll be born bent in eight places. Then Kahoda went to the court of King Janaka, lost a debate to the court's champion, and never came home. The boy was born bent, just as the curse said.
They called him Ashtavakra: eight bends. At twelve he learned what had happened, and set out, crooked and limping, for that court to win his father back.

teach.h: THE COURT LAUGHS AT THE BODY.
teach.b: In the Mahabharata's telling, the boy talks his way past the gatekeeper, defeats the court's champion debater, and his father is restored.

People love to tell a popular addition: when Ashtavakra walked in, the courtiers laughed at his body, and he laughed back. Why are you laughing? they asked. I thought this was an assembly of the wise, he said.

You only judge the skin. Whether that exchange is old or newer, it's the jnana teaching in one joke: the atman, the real self, is not the body. A twelve-year-old in a crooked body had out-argued the champion.
It fits the book that carries his name. The Ashtavakra Gita is a short Sanskrit dialogue between the sage and King Janaka. Nobody knows when it was written, or by whom.
It opens with the king asking three questions.
Paraphrased: how is knowledge gained? How will freedom come? How is detachment reached?
Tell me this, my lord. How do I know. How am I free.

How do I let go. And notice who's asking: a king, with everything. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna names Janaka as one who reached perfection through action, a king who lived in the world and wasn't owned by it.
The answer he gets, tomorrow, doesn't ask him to give up his throne. And today?

teach.h: THE SELF IS NOT THE SKIN.
teach.b: We still size each other up by skin: height, color, a limp, a wheelchair, a bad photo.

how: The Ashtavakra Gita is read and chanted in many Advaita circles as a direct statement of non-dual teaching, often studied alongside the Upanishads; its opening questions from King Janaka frame the whole text.

o: a path of strict purity rules and customs
knowing the self, which is not the body
a path of winning debates with clever words

games.q: Ashtavakra and Janaka — tap the pairs.

s: the date of the Ashtavakra Gita is well established
nobody knows when it was written, or by whom.
Ashtavakra's story appears in the Mahabharata
the Mahabharata tells of his curse, his journey to Janaka's court, and his father's return.
Janaka's questions are about how to get to heaven
he asks how knowledge comes, how freedom comes, and how detachment is reached.

games.q: you're a twelve-year-old bent in eight places. the whole royal court laughs when you walk in. in the popular story, what do you do?
o: laugh back, and call them leather-workers.
ask the king to silence them.
games.why: he laughs back: he'd expected the wise, and found people who judge only the skin.

practice: Ask Janaka's three questions for yourself, slowly, one per stretch of breathing: what do I actually know, for certain, right now? Where do I feel not free, just noticing, not fixing?
What am I gripping, a plan, a person, an idea of myself? Let each question open without rushing an answer; the asking is the practice.

wordCard.voice: Jnana yoga, through the Ashtavakra Gita: a dialogue between a sage bent in eight places and King Janaka, who asks how to know, how to be free, how to let go.

orig.note: Sanskrit: ashta (eight) + vakra (bent, crooked): the sage's name.

carryVoice: Your line: the self is not the skin. The courtiers laughed, and saw only the body. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (the story of Ashtavakra, Kahoda and Bandi at Janaka's court)
Bhagavad Gita 3.20 (Janaka and others reached perfection through action)
